items.title: New York Yankees @ San Diego Padres: Carlos Rodón vs. Robbie Ray
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Friday night was a tough pill for the Yankees to swallow, losing to the Padres in extra innings after managing to take the lead against arguably the game’s most dominant reliever. With the Rays marching onward atop the AL East, knotting up this series is crucial, and the team will need to quickly move on from that hard loss yesterday. They face yet another left-handed pitcher in Robbie Ray, and counter with a southpaw of their own in a national-broadcast faceoff from San Diego.

Because it’s me, and the Baseball Gods (or just my editors) have it out for me personally, I am once again doomed to cover a Carlos Rodón start. I must once again attempt to reconcile his actual performance on the field, which has been quite good as long as he’s been healthy in 2026, with how unpleasant I find watching him pitch. He’d be on pace for a three-win season if he didn’t have those two IL stints, with a 3.20 ERA and 3.74 FIP that both go just fine with being the No. 4 pitcher in a rotation this deep.

Rodón has gone just 12.2 innings in his three starts since that most recent IL trip, as the team seems committed to making sure recovery is permanent, at least for 2026. In those three outings though, he’s been dynamite from an ERA basis with a 2.84, even if the walks have been a problem. Command is often the last thing to return after injury, and getting the ball in the strike zone will need to be a priority for Carlos today.

Ray, meanwhile, has had a weird year split between the Giants and Padres. He’s suppressed runs well, with a Pi ERA, but he’s put up the second-lowest strikeout rate in a full season of his career as well as a walk rate a point and a half above his career baseline. There’s a bit of a Robbie Ray bubble, and the Yankees could turn around some of their LHP misfortune this year by popping it.

Paul Goldschmidt returns to the top of the lineup and starts at first base today, while Ben Rice moves down to cleanup after his big night on Friday. So-called lefty specialist Amed Rosario will be at second base, but the Yankees have clearly seen the writing on the wall with righty-hitting Ali Sánchez, and will start Austin Wells behind the plate. The hometown(-ish) kid Spencer Jones is back in center as well, with Trent Grisham going on the IL and Jasson Domínguez taking Grisham’s roster spot.

It’s a Yankee game on a weekend, so there’s gotta be one national broadcast in the mix. Tonight’s contest is on FOX.

: Petco Park – San Diego, CA

: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 – NYY | KWFN 97.3, XEMO 860 – SD

items.title: The best errors in Yankees’ history
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
Last Sunday, there was quite a hubbub surrounding a catch/no catch call in the Yankees-Red Sox game. Ceddanne Rafaela came very close to making a catch on a Jazz Chisholm Jr. fly ball that then would’ve led to a double play. However, the call on the field was that he trapped it, and that ruling was upheld on replay. A seemingly rattled Red Sox team then gave up five runs in the innings and ended up getting crushed by the Yankees. The victory gave New York the season series over Boston, which could come into play should the teams end up tied after the regular season.

We’ll never truly know how much that call and subsequent replay ruling actually did rattle the Red Sox, but it did get me thinking. I was wondering about the time where a set of mistakes by the other teams proved the costliest. It’s hard to argue against an instance of that happening in a World Series Game 7, so I think this might be it.

Having been down 3-1 in the series, the Yankees won Game 5 and 6 against the Milwaukee Braves to force a winner-take-all finale of the 1958 World Series. The Braves struck first against Don Larsen, with a run scoring on a Wes Covington groundout in the bottom of the first inning.

Braves’ starter Lew Burdette had been the hero when the two teams met in the Fall Classic in 1957. Burdette was the winning pitcher in Games 2, 5, and 7. The last two were both shutouts as Burdette was named Series MVP. This time luck wasn’t quite on his side.

In the top of the second, Yogi Berra led off the inning with a walk. Elston Howard was up next and he laid down a bunt attempt. Milwaukee first baseman Frank Torre — brother future Yankee skipper Joe; Frank famously received a heart transplant during the 1996 World Series — fielded the bunt. However, Torre’s throw to a covering Burdette at first was poor and got away. Howard was safe and Berra ended up at third.

Next up was Yankees’ third baseman Jerry Lumpe. He too hit a soft groundedr to Torre, this one of the unintentional kind. Torre once again fielded it, but this throw to Burdette was also off. A high effort allowed everyone to be safe, loading the bases. The next two batters both hit into outs, but both were good enough to score runs, giving the Yankees a lead that was only partly of their own doing.

Now, those two plays on their own did not win the Yankees the game and the series, but the Bombers never trailed again after that. Larsen got himself into some trouble in the third, eventually making way for Bob Turley. Del Crandall did tie the game for the Braves with a sixth inning homer, but other than that, Turley was excellent, throwing 6.2 innings out of the bullpen, allowing just that one run on two hits.

Turley’s performance eventually allowed the Yankees to breakthrough in the eighth. Howard was involved again, hitting an RBI single to give the Yankees the lead. However, the big play came a couple batters later when Bill Skowron hit a massive three-run homer off Burdette. The Yankees are blessed with many clutch moments throughout history, because for many other teams, that Skowron homer would be the singular best moment in franchise history. Meanwhile, it gets lost in the shuffle a bit for the Yankees.

Obviously, there was quite a bit of crucial moments following Torre’s two errors in the third, but there’s no way to accurately predict what happens if he just makes those plays cleanly. That being said, not only did they lead to two runs immediately after, but that was a bunch more pitches Burdette had to throw in that inning. They probably added a bit of fatigue that the Yankees then took advantage of later on. They may not have been the singular difference, but it’s hard to say they weren’t one.

items.title: Yankees place Trent Grisham on IL with hamstring strain, recall Jasson Domínguez
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The Yankees lost in walk-off fashion to San Diego on Friday night, but they might not have played extras had it not been for a misplay that allowed the Padres to score their only run of the initial nine innings. With two outs in the second, Xander Bogaerts got under a pitch from Max Fried on what could charitably be described as a flare to center. It was a ball that most center fielders would’ve at minimum come close to and have the chance for a diving catch.

But for the Yankees, Trent Grisham was in center field, and while he was once an elite defender, he has been far from that in 2026. It didn’t help that he was playing a guy with an 82 OPS+ and only 11 homers far too deep, but regardless, he was clearly not moving well on the play. The ball dipped in with ease and Ty France scored. When the half-inning ended, Grisham spoke to the team trainer and disappeared down the dugout tunnel. Soon, the Yankees announced that Grisham was dealing with discomfort in his right hamstring, the same one that sent him to the IL earlier in 2026. It’s been an uneven year on the whole for Grisham, who has hit .211/.308/.395 with 18 homers but only a 95 OPS+.

Now, we know that Grisham is indeed heading back to the IL. Jasson Domínguez will fly from Scranton to San Diego to rejoin the team and take Grisham’s spot on the roster. The former top prospect had an injury of his own earlier in 2026, but when given the chance to play, he did not acquit himself well, batting just .230/.270/.380 with a 79 OPS+ and exactly 0.0 rWAR.

It might only be a short-term stay for Domínguez since it seems like Aaron Judge is tracking to return to the team soon (though New York has made no announcements) and there’s only so much roster flexibility at the moment. But for now, Domínguez will serve as outfield depth, though Spencer Jones will likely get the lion’s share of time in center with Grisham out. Cody Bellinger is a candidate for some center field time as well, though he did bang himself up a bit on a foul ball last night too.

items.title: Checking in on the Yankees’ August additions, one month later
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
The New York Yankees didn’t really make too much noise before the 2026 trade deadline. They added a slugging first baseman in Luis García Jr., an outfielder in Heliot Ramos, and not much else. They failed to bring in significant additions to the rotation and bullpen, which was ‘addressed’ with cheap free-agent signing Michael Fulmer and waiver claim John Schreiber well after August 3.

For this exercise, let’s focus on the major trades, namely García and Ramos, and a third player who was called up from Triple-A Scranton but has been, essentially and for all intents and purposes, a post-deadline acquisition: shortstop George Lombard Jr.

The lefty slugger has been the best player the Bombers acquired at or around the trade deadline. The 26-year-old masher started his breakout in the nation’s capital and continued it in the Bronx. He has hit, before Friday’s game, a robust .292/.337/.500 with five home runs and a 132 wRC+ in pinstripes.

García had flirted with above-average power numbers in the past, but he had never put together such a strong season until 2026, making him a bit of a gamble for the Yankees. So far, it’s safe to say it has paid off big-time, as he has given the team a reliable, productive left-handed slugger to plug and play in the middle of the lineup.

During times when the Yanks missed some key power hitters, including the still-absent Aaron Judge, García has proved to be a useful hitter.

While García’s arrival has been a hit, the same can’t be said about Ramos. The outfielder is struggling to the tune of a .141/.286/.266 with a home run, a 27.3 percent strikeout rate, a 61 wRC+, and -0.5 fWAR. He has been with the Yankees for a month, yet he’s already their least valuable position player by fWAR.

If we see Ramos’ performance with the Yankees without context, he has been a disaster. However, it’s important to point out that since August 20, he has been hitting a solid .227/.370/.455 with a homer, two doubles, and a 136 wRC+ in 27 plate appearances. His expected stats also suggest he’s been quite unlucky in New York; he’s got a perfectly solid .338 expected wOBA as a Yankee. See, for instance, the hardest-hit double play ball in the majors this year:

Perhaps if we give him some more time, his overall stat line would look a lot better.

Ramos isn’t much of a defender, and he isn’t particularly fast, either, but in time, he’ll prove that he’s a fine hitter with power. His role will undoubtedly diminish when Aaron Judge returns from injury, though.

The Yankees decided to start the Lombard clock on August 4, right after the deadline. And what a ride it has been. He started his MLB tenure on fire, with highlight-reel defensive plays and two homers in his first four games.

After a few weeks, his offensive performance started to diminish, and he had a .253/.310/.367 line with a 90 wRC+ on Tuesday, when he had to depart a game after injuring his knee. He dodged a bullet and, after missing a few days, returned to the lineup on Friday.

The Yankees are committed to letting him develop at the MLB level. After all, he made light work of Double-A and Triple-A pitchers this year.

Lombard is the Yankees’ shortstop of the future. He’s an extremely young player, and he may make mistakes in bunches, but the potential is there for him to impact games both offensively and defensively (and on the basepaths, too) for a long time.

items.title: In praise of the high number
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
I’m a personal believer in wearing the lowest possible number as a player. No infielder should have a number greater than 25, and 25 should only be worn by a first baseman. Numbers in the 30s and 40s are for pitchers, and your outfielders fill out the rest. That is the Way Baseball Numbers Should Work.

Of course, the Yankees have retired 21 numbers, every single one-digit, and 15 of those 21 are below #25 — yes, I’m finally correctly counting Whitey Ford, who I always forget when listing off the retirees by memory. Add that to the 25 other guys that are on the present roster, when you get added to the big-league club there aren’t that many options to put on your back. In 2016, Aaron Judge ran into this problem, eventually deciding to keep the #99 issued to him in spring training. That #99 will likely be the next number the Yankees retire, and I think it’s a part of what’s made him one of the faces of baseball over the past decade.

Now we have a pair of rookies filling out the middle of the Yankee order, both of them sporting unusual jersey numbers for much the same reason that Judge did. George Lombard Jr. is #96 and Spencer Jones #78, George one of three MLB players to sport those digits this year and one of them was Quad-A relief depth Yovanny Cruz for these same Yankees. Jones wears a slightly more popular number, even if I only know one of the other guys who share 78:

And despite my penchant for lower numbers (I’m #24 myself), I love what Lombard and Jones have done, even if it was by accident. It’s difficult to stand out on the current Yankee roster — ok, it’s difficult to stand out on what the ideal current Yankee roster is. Even if you’re a threeish win player, pretty good, you’re going to end up behind the big three in the rotation, Cody Bellinger, Ben Rice, Jazz Chisholm Jr. and of course the captain himself. This goes triple when you try and stand out in the annals of Yankee history itself.

#78 and 96 allow the youngsters to carve out a bit of their own identity, just a little. It probably isn’t going to last. Ben Rice was issued #93 for his first taste of MLB in 2024, and once he carved out a permanent role for himself on the team switched to the much more sensible, and aesthetically pleasing, #22. If Jazz doesn’t return to the team this winter, #13 becomes an obvious option for George if he can stick to the roster, ditto for #12 if the club lets Trent Grisham walk. #78 is a little more of a reasonable number albeit one more for relievers than starting centerfielders, but it wouldn’t be surprising to see Jones switch down as well.

With a club as numerically complicated as the Yankees, picking something a little funky and unconventional makes me like you just a little more — indeed, perhaps more than GLJ’s current performance deserves. We’ve seen how Judge has been able to take a strange jersey assignment and make it his own. I’m not asking either Spencer or George to be Aaron Judge, just to want to be as much of an individual in an org that sometimes squashes that.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Al Orth
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
There are several forgotten heroes from Yankees’ baseball prior to when the franchise started to win championships. Not that they didn’t have good years as a team in that time, but the pre-Babe Ruth years tend to blend together in a lot of fans’ minds.

One of those forgotten heroes was Al Orth, whose 1906 could be in the discussion for best seasons by a Yankee pitcher.

September 5, 1872 (Sedalia, MO) October 8, 1948 (Lynchburg, VA) 1904-09

While he was born in Missouri, Al Orth lived much of his early life in Indiana. There’s not a ton out there about his early life other than that he eventually attended DePauw University in Greencastle, IN. At some point, he developed an ability for baseball and begins showing up in on minor league rosters at 22-years-old, playing for the Lynchburg Hill Climbers in 1895.

In Lynchburg, Orth very quickly began to catch the eye of major league teams. After 269 good innings in 1895, Lynchburg sold him to the Phillies later that season. He went on to debut and throw 88 more innings in Philly that year, and put up a very solid, for that year, 3.89 ERA.

Over the next several years, while he had his ups and down, Orth became a fixture on the Phillies’ roster, and a mostly solid one at that. Known as the “Curveless Wonder,” Orth got his success from just varying the speed of his pitches as opposed to getting great movement. With the exceptions of 1895-96 — when he was still breaking into the bigs — and 1899, Orth threw at least 250 innings every season in Philadelphia and also posted at least 14 wins in all except his debut 1895. However, the Phillies never really got all that close to a NL pennant in his time there.

Orth had his best year as a Phillie in 1901. That year, he went 20-12 with a 2.27 ERA (151 ERA+), and recorded a league high six complete game shutouts. However, something else also happened in 1901: the American League was founded. Many NL mainstays started making the jump over, and Orth did so too, joining the Washington Senators for a reported $3500.

Despite moving to the still developing league from the “Senior Circuit,” Orth struggled in Washington. In 84 appearances over three seasons with the Senators, ho posted a 4.21 ERA, which equated to a 79 ERA+, as baseball began to enter the “deadball era.” He dropped off even further in 1904, leading to a July trade that sent him to the New York Highlanders.

The move to the Highlanders led to a rejuvenation for Orth. He was much better over the rest of 1904 — helping New York nearly swipe the AL pennant — and was again solid in 1905. Then in 1906, he put together his best career season. In New York, Orth joined a pitching staff that featured “spitballer” Jack Chesbro. With help from Chesbro, Orth began to throw the spitball himself, leading to a standout 1906. In a league-leading 338.2 innings, Orth put up a 2.34 ERA (127 ERA+), with 27 wins. According to modern stats, Orth was worth 8.1 rWAR and 6.0 fWAR, putting him among the league’s best that season.

Orth was okay the next year, but the Highlanders fell way back in the standings, and Orth ended up leading the league in losses. It was the first time ever a pitcher went from having the most wins to the most losses in consecutive years. After an even worse year in 1908, Orth seemingly left the majors, moved to Virginia and was set to be a player-manager in the Virginia League.

However, new Highlanders’ manager George Stallings lured Orth back for 1909. He only threw three innings on the mound and instead filled a new role. Orth had always been a pretty solid hitter, and not even for just pitcher standards, with a career 92 OPS+. Stallings used Orth as a pinch-hitter and in a handful of games at second base, and he put up a 113 OPS+ for the year.

Following that season, Orth did leave the majors and played for a couple minor league teams, including back in his new home in Lynchburg. He then returned to the majors in 1912, albeit as an umpire. He was the home plate ump for a 1912 game where pitchers Hippo Vaughn and Fred Toney both had no-hitters through nine innings. Toney completed his in 10 innings, after his Reds’ teammates scored a run on two hits in the top of the 10th.

Orth was a NL ump through 1917, at which point he left that role. Back in Virginia, he had stints as the baseball coaches at Washington & Lee University and the Virginia Military Institute. He resided in the area until his death in 1948 at age 76.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Rays, Red Sox both gain ground; Guardians sweep doubleheader
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The Yankees lost a tough one on Friday night, as they failed to score more than a Ben Rice solo shot against old nemesis Walker Buehler, and while Max Fried, Will Warren, and David Bednar admirably went toe-to-toe with a fierce Padres bullpen, it wasn’t enough. A 2-1 lead in the 10th vanished on one mighty swing of the bat by Luis Campusano against Paul Blackburn, who entered play with a 1.62 ERA. No shade at the pitching in this one, the offense just had to do more early on with Buehler. He’s better than he was in his nightmare 2025 with Boston, but not much better.

Here’s what else was afoot around the Junior Circuit on Friday. The loss was costly.

Tampa Bay Rays (84-57) 7, Texas Rangers (70-72) 6

Texas helped New York gain a half-game on the Thursday offday by blanking Tampa Bay 6-0, but six runs weren’t enough for the Rangers to be of any use on Friday. The Rays jumped back to four games ahead of the Yankees, doing most of their damage against former top prospect Kumar Rocker in a bulk relief appearance. Ezequiel Duran briefly gave Texas a 1-0 lead in the second, only for Tampa Bay to counter with six unanswered runs between the third and the fifth. Jonathan Aranda and Richie Palacios both hit solo shots, and in the fifth, Aranda sandwiched a double between two-baggers from Yandy Díaz and Junior Caminero.

Victor Mesa Jr. also had an RBI knock in the fifth as Tampa Bay’s lead grew to 6-1.

Give credit to the Rangers’ No. 9 hitter, catcher Elias Díaz. He is the primary reason why the Rays had to sweat this one out late. In the seventh, Texas drove Nick Martinez from the game with a one-out walk from Jake Burger and an Evan Carter single. Garrett Cleavinger entered, walked Cody Freeman to load the bases, and then coughed up a game-changing grand slam to Díaz.

As it turned out, the Rays needed the insurance run they got with one down in the ninth. Yandy singled off Trade Deadline acquisition Chase Silseth, Jorge Mateo pinch-ran and stole second, and after Aranda got plunked, Caminero drove in Mateo with a hit to center. Adam Macko then entered and stranded the runners, making it a 7-5 ballgame to begin the bottom of the ninth.

The Rangers had life in the ninth when Bryan Baker issued back-to-back walks to the first two batters; he was forced from the game rather quickly due to illness with his velocity down, too. Tyler Wells had to get the last three outs, and he pulled it off. Pinch-hitter Nicky Lopez bunted the runners into scoring position, Díaz played his fifth run with a sacrifice fly, and Justin Foscue popped up a 2-1 pitch to end it.

Boston Red Sox (77-65) 1, Baltimore Orioles (69-73) 0: I don’t know how many of you caught the Chris Sale shutout against the Dodgers a little over a week ago, but it played out in a somewhat-similar manner to this Red Sox/O’s game last night. Drake Baldwin led off that one with a homer off Yoshinobu Yamamoto for the first and only run of the night. Yamamoto was otherwise brilliant but LA never dented home plate against Sale and it was a 1-0 final.

Well, Ranger Suarez didn’t go as deep as Sale and Mickey Gasper homered on the second at-bat of the game rather than the first, but otherwise … pretty close! (Although I suppose Braves/Dodgers didn’t have the same benches-clearing feistiness.) Boston won its second straight one-run game at Camden Yards, with Suarez firing seven shutout frames before Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman slammed the door. The O’s only three at-bats all night with a runner in scoring position, and none resulted in hits. Shane Baz and the Baltimore bullpen did a very nice job, but no cigar. They’re in serious trouble now, losing a game and a half to Cleveland in the Wild Card race in one day, falling to three back. Meanwhile, Boston is 3.5 behind New York for the top Wild Card spot.

Chicago White Sox (74-67) 4, Minnesota Twins (67-74) 1: Chicago’s AL Central lead would be trimmed by half a game due to circumstances beyond their control, but the Pale Hose won their own game against the Twins. Miguel Vargas, Braden Montgomery, and Colson Montgomery all flexed their muscles with blasts off Zebby Matthews, and the White Sox threw shutout ball until the ninth. Vargas and Colson each registered their 30th homers of the season. Incidentally, we have not been tracking the Twins for a moment, but at 4.5 games behind Cleveland for the Wild Card with three teams ahead of them, they are all but toast.

Cleveland Guardians (71-70) 7, Detroit Tigers (64-76) 6 [Game 1] The perhaps-no-longer-Gritty Tigs’ season is utterly lost at this point, so they have to settle for trying to play spoiler for the team that rallied from a record 15.5 games down to swipe the AL Central from them in 2025. And they took a 6-2 lead in Cleveland by beating up on Logan Allen with two-run knocks from Ben Malgeri and Max Clark, as well as a solo shot by Spencer Torkelson. However, the doubleheader matinee turned into The Brayan Rocchio Show. He crushed a game-tying grand slam off Keider Montero in the fourth, and with it still knotted at 6-6 in the ninth, he launched the longest homer of his career to walk it off.

Cleveland Guardians (72-70) 4, Detroit Tigers (64-77) 3 [10 innings] [Game 2] The Guardos had so much fun walking the Tigers off in the opener that they decided to do it all over again in the nightcap. Once again, Detroit had the early advantage, tallying three off Trade Deadline acquisition Foster Griffin. The Guardians crawled back, and 2024 No. 1 pick Travis Bazzana swatted a two-run homer in the eighth to knot it up at 3-3. Bazzana must have taken notes from Rocchio because he got to tally the walk-off as well as that game-tying blast. Hunter Gaddis stranded the zombie runner in the top of the 10th with three groundouts, opening the door for Bazzana to end it on a single off Kenley Jansen with Rocchio on third following a pair of stolen bases. Cleveland’s twin bill sweep lifted their Wild Card lead to a game over Toronto.

Toronto Blue Jays (71-71) 9, Kansas City Royals (63-79) 2: Cleveland winning twice with the doubleheader always meant that the Jays would be losing ground of some kind to them in their late Wild Card chase. But they at least limited the damage to a half-game loss. Although old friend/two-time Tommy John surgery recipient Jameson Taillon had to leave with dreaded elbow discomfort, his offense picked him up. Everyone in the starting lineup outside of Charles McAdoo had at least one hit, with Ernie Clement, Alejandro Kirk, and George Springer all delivering RBI doubles.

Houston Astros (73-69) 3, Arizona Diamondbacks (74-68) 1: Not much to touch on from this one because neither of these teams are very interesting. Cristian Javier fired five frames of one-hit, one-run ball, fanning eight, and batterymate Yainer Diaz kicked off the scoring for Houston with a solo shot against Merrill Kelly. The ’Stros tacked on more in the third when Isaac Paredes doubled in Jeremy Peña, and Jose Altuve plated Yordan Alvarez on a sacrifice fly. The Rangers’ loss means that Houston has a fairly comfortable three-game lead, aided by an Astros edge in the head-to-head tiebreaker.

items.title: The Yankees Reliever Confidence Index: September Edition
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
As the Yankees enter the season’s final month, a bullpen that’s been a strength throughout the year is running on fumes. Injuries to Fernando Cruz and Kervin Castro have further strained an already thin unit, forcing the Yankees to get creative in adding some veteran talent from outside their organization for the stretch run.

As I do each month in a given season, I’m going to take a look at the Yankees’ relievers to identify how manager Aaron Boone is deploying each and offer a verdict as to how much trust we can place in them moving forward using the following ranking system:

  • : As confident as one can be in a reliever, the most fickle position in baseball
  • : High degree of confidence, but some trepidation remains
  • : Glass half full or glass half empty? The choice is yours
  • : Major concerns here, though perhaps a glimmer of hope
  • : Absolute zero — usually reserved for those with a minimal track record

Statistics below are from August 6-September 2.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP, Saves (in 7 opportunities)

After a couple of days off and with the rest of the bullpen gassed, Bednar came in to eat the eighth inning of what was then a 7-1 blowout at the hands of the Angels on Monday. He allowed three runs, inflating his stats in garbage time. The right-hander allowed only one other earned run all August, though, cementing his status as one of the game’s most reliable closers.

No one in baseball has finished more games than Bednar’s 50 this year, and he’s done it while blowing just three saves. He isn’t as flashy as some of the game’s other elite late-inning arms, but he’s been as effective as any of them.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

It’s been a choppier month than we’ve seen before from Headrick this year. Opponents hit .345 with a 1.015 OPS against him in August, a red flag for a pitcher who’s made the second-most appearances in baseball. Still, even after his uneven stretch, the southpaw’s ERA sits below 2.00.

Headrick has shown enough to receive the benefit of the doubt here. Especially after the injury to Cruz, who was among MLB’s most-used relievers before his injury, fatigue is a legitimate concern. But in a tight AL East race, expect Boone to continue deploying his fireman in big spots.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

It’s been a rapid ascent for Blackburn, who began the season as the last man out of the bullpen and is now one of Boone’s most trusted relievers. He hasn’t skipped a beat since moving into a high-leverage role, allowing no earned runs across his last 16 appearances dating back to late July.

Like other Yankees reclamation projects before him, Blackburn has been able to leverage his sinker into a skyrocketing ground ball rate. There’s no reason at this point to believe the tweaks he’s made are not sustainable.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

A week and change ago, Fulmer was out of a job after the Angels cut him loose. Now, he’s the Yankees’ new shiny toy, with the Joel Sherman relaying that the team feels they saw things in his video that other teams missed. With a dearth of options, he’s been thrown right into the fire. The early results have not been encouraging.

Fulmer has only made four appearance for the Yankees, so it’s too soon to say how valuable he will be. Any return to form would be a remarkable comeback for the 33-year-old, who’s appeared only sporadically in MLB since 2023.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

Formerly ol’ reliable in this column, Hill’s stock took a major hit after a disastrous run from mid-May through mid-July in which he allowed 18 runs in 18 innings. He’s been better since, deployed strategically in mostly in lower-leverage spots.

Hill is not a back-end reliever, and that should be OK. The crafty lefty still serves a useful role, particularly against lefty batters, who are hitting .205 with a .575 OPS against him this year.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP (with Kansas City and New York)

Another new kid on the block, Schreiber made his Yankees debut on Tuesday, pitching a clean ninth to close out a victory against the Angels. The 32-year-old brings with him a long track record of steady bullpen performance, including this season. Schreiber posted a 3.65 ERA and 117 ERA+ in 56 appearances with Kansas City before they placed him on waivers as they drifted out of contention.

Some of Schreiber’s underlying metrics — including a .254 BABIP and 36:22 K:BB ratio with Kansas City — are cause for concern. Still, considering the Yankees got him for nothing, he’s a quality pickup given the slim pickings at this point in the season.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

Yarbrough has been something of a shadow starter for most of the season, appearing once a week or so to pitch multiple innings in relief and then retreating to obscurity in the bullpen. A four-run blowup against the Red Sox last week jumped his season ERA nearly a half-run, underscoring the limits of his bag of tricks.

Come playoff time, Yarbrough should only be seeing action if a game is out of hand. He’s been a perfectly serviceable placeholder this year, helping eat innings in a bullpen that’s seen its high performers used frequently.

: IP, ERA, SO (including minor leagues)

Gil’s wilderness period is over. After a disastrous start to the year for the Yankees and nearly four months spent on the IL, the team decided to bring their former Rookie of the Year back in a relief role. He tossed 7.1 scoreless innings across five appearances in the minors, and he made his return to the big leagues last Monday, allowing one run in two innings of work.

Gil’s is such a bizarre case that it’s difficult to place any stock in him. While unquestionably talented, the 27-year-old has endured consecutive lost seasons. Until he can prove otherwise, his superlative 2024 campaign is the clear outlier. Time will tell if he can reinvent himself in his new role.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 9/5/26
items.author: Jake Devin
items.content:
The Yankees played their second extra-innings thriller in as many games, and it looked like they might pull it out yet again. They scratched across a run in the tenth against Padres super closer Mason Miller, and they went to Paul Blackburn to close out the game, only to see Luis Campusano end the game with one swing. The loss stung, the Rays having won earlier in the night 7-6 in Texas. The AL East deficit stands at four.

On the site today, Josh writes in praise of the high number, like the ones rookies George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones are sporting on the back of their uniforms. Andrew goes through yesterday’s Rivalry Roundup, while today’s Yankee Birthday feature is on Al Orth, a pitcher from the earliest days of the franchise. Also, Nick delivers this month’s Reliever Confidence Index, and Andrés recaps how the additions the Yankees made at the beginning of August have done in their first month as Yankees.

New York Yankees at San Diego Padres

Venue: Petco Park, San Diego, CA

1. If Trent Grisham hit the IL with his latest hamstring injury, should Spencer Jones be the starting center fielder from here on out?

2. Do you think Will Warren’s work in a piggyback role last night is a precursor to the Yankees moving him to the bullpen in the coming weeks?
